```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| echo: false
#| edit: false
#| output: false
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Hidden setup — runs automatically when the page opens.
# Everything DESeq2 / dada2 / kallisto produced was pre-computed and saved as
# small CSVs; here we just read them in.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

counts_df <- read.csv("data/counts.csv", check.names = FALSE)
annot     <- read.csv("data/annotation.csv")
meta      <- read.csv("data/metadata.csv")
sf_deseq  <- read.csv("data/size_factors.csv")
vst_df    <- read.csv("data/vst.csv", check.names = FALSE)
de        <- read.csv("data/de_APP_vs_CON.csv")
de_cih    <- read.csv("data/de_CIH_vs_CON.csv")
gene_sets <- read.csv("data/gene_sets.csv")
qual      <- read.csv("data/quality_profiles.csv")
retention <- read.csv("data/read_retention.csv")
kal       <- read.csv("data/kallisto_summary.csv")

# --- count matrix: genes in rows, samples in columns -----------------------
CNT <- as.matrix(counts_df[, -1])
rownames(CNT) <- counts_df$gene
mode(CNT) <- "integer"

# --- variance-stabilised matrix (what DESeq2's vst() returned) -------------
VST <- as.matrix(vst_df[, -1])
rownames(VST) <- vst_df$gene

samples   <- colnames(CNT)                       # CON1..IL3
condition <- meta$condition[match(samples, meta$sample)]
cond_col  <- c(CON = "#4C72B0", APP = "#DD8452", CIH = "#55A868", IL = "#C44E52")

# --- quick lookup: gene id -> functional annotation ------------------------
ann <- setNames(annot$annotation, annot$gene)
ann[is.na(ann) | ann == "" | ann == "---NA---"] <- "no annotation"

# --- feedback helper used by the fill-in-the-blank cells -------------------
say <- function(ok, right, hint) {
  if (isTRUE(ok)) cat("\n✅ ", right, "\n", sep = "")
  else            cat("\n\U0001F4A1 ", hint, "\n", sep = "")
  invisible(NULL)
}

cat(sprintf("Data loaded: %d genes x %d samples.\n", nrow(CNT), ncol(CNT)))
```

# How this page works

Module 2 has two kinds of work in it, and this page keeps them clearly apart.

::: {.runs-here}
Cells like this **run in your browser**. There is nothing to install and nothing to
break — edit the code, press **Run**, and the result appears underneath. Where you
see `______` you have to fill something in; running the cell tells you whether you
got it right.
:::

::: {.run-local}
Blocks like this **cannot run in a browser**. `DESeq2`, `dada2` and `kallisto` are
not available here — they need a real R installation or a terminal. Copy this code
into **RStudio on ERDA** and run it there. Each block lists exactly which files you
need and where to get them on Absalon.
:::

The two are not alternatives. The browser cells are where you learn *what the method
does and how to read its output*; the local blocks are where you actually run the
pipeline on real files, which is what the group assignment and the exam expect of you.

::: {.provenance}
Every number on this page comes from the real Module 2 dataset: RNAseq of the fungal
plant pathogen *Colletotrichum fructicola* (Liang et al. 2018, *BMC Genomics* 19:557),
four growth forms with three replicates each — **CON** conidia, **APP** appressoria,
**CIH** cellophane infectious hyphae, **IL** infected apple leaf.

The quality profiles were computed from the actual FASTQ files, the abundances are
real kallisto output, and the differential expression results were produced by
DESeq2's algorithm on the full count matrix. **One exception, stated plainly:** the
gene sets in Session 4 are *keyword-derived* functional categories built from the
annotation text (all genes whose description matches `cytochrome p450`, and so on).
They are not curated GO or PFAM terms. The enrichment *method* you practise is
exactly the real one; the categories are a stand-in, because this genome has no
curated GO annotation shipped with the course data.
:::

# Session 1 — Read quality control {#sec-qc}
[Monday 21-09]{.session-chip}

Before anything is mapped or counted, you have to look at the reads and decide what
to throw away. That decision is the whole point of this session — `filterAndTrim()`
is just the function that carries it out.

::: {.run-local}
**Get the data.** On Absalon, Module 2 → Exercises → `C_fructicola_GSE103878_small.zip`
(139 MB). Unzip it into your working directory on ERDA.

::: {.filelist}
C_fructicola_GSE103878_small/
&nbsp;&nbsp;APP1small_SRR6041847_1.fastq.gz &nbsp; APP1small_SRR6041847_2.fastq.gz
&nbsp;&nbsp;... 18 files total = 9 samples x 2 mates (forward `_1`, reverse `_2`)
:::

```r
library(dada2)
path  <- "~/Rworkdir/C_fructicola_small"     # adjust to your own path
list.files(path)

# Sort forward and reverse files so the two vectors stay in the same sample order
fnFs <- sort(list.files(path, pattern = "_1.fastq.gz", full.names = TRUE))
fnRs <- sort(list.files(path, pattern = "_2.fastq.gz", full.names = TRUE))

plotQualityProfile(fnFs[1:2])    # forward reads
plotQualityProfile(fnRs[1:2])    # reverse reads
```

Those two plots are what the next cells reproduce here, from the same files.
:::

## 1.1 The quality profile

`plotQualityProfile()` draws one thing: the distribution of Phred quality scores at
each position (cycle) along the read. We pre-computed that summary for all 18 files.

```{webr}
# One row per sample x mate x cycle.
head(qual, 3)

# Look at the forward reads (mate 1) of sample CON1
q1 <- qual[qual$sample == "CON1" & qual$mate == 1, ]

plot(q1$cycle, q1$mean_q, type = "n",
     ylim = c(20, 42), xlab = "Cycle (position along the read)",
     ylab = "Phred quality score", main = "CON1 forward reads")
# the interquartile band: 25th-75th percentile of quality at each cycle
polygon(c(q1$cycle, rev(q1$cycle)), c(q1$q25, rev(q1$q75)),
        col = adjustcolor("#2f7d4f", 0.18), border = NA)
lines(q1$cycle, q1$mean_q, lwd = 2, col = "#2f7d4f")
abline(h = 30, lty = 2, col = "red")     # Q30 = 1 error in 1000 bases
legend("bottomleft", c("mean Q", "Q25-Q75 band", "Q30"), bty = "n",
       lty = c(1, NA, 2), lwd = c(2, NA, 1), pch = c(NA, 15, NA),
       col = c("#2f7d4f", adjustcolor("#2f7d4f", 0.3), "red"))
```

Two features are typical of Illumina data and both matter for what you do next: the
first few cycles are noisier, and quality decays towards the 3' end.

## 1.2 Forward versus reverse reads

```{webr}
# Fill in the mate number for the REVERSE reads.
mate_rev <- ______            # <- blank

fwd <- qual[qual$sample == "CON1" & qual$mate == 1,        ]
rev <- qual[qual$sample == "CON1" & qual$mate == mate_rev, ]

plot(fwd$cycle, fwd$mean_q, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#4C72B0", ylim = c(20, 42),
     xlab = "Cycle", ylab = "Mean Phred quality", main = "CON1: forward vs reverse")
lines(rev$cycle, rev$mean_q, lwd = 2, col = "#C44E52")
abline(h = 30, lty = 2)
legend("bottomleft", c("forward (_1)", "reverse (_2)"), lwd = 2,
       col = c("#4C72B0", "#C44E52"), bty = "n")

cat("mean quality  forward:", round(mean(fwd$mean_q), 2),
    " reverse:", round(mean(rev$mean_q), 2), "\n")

say(identical(mate_rev, 2),
    "reverse reads are mate 2 — and they are consistently worse than the forward reads. That is normal: the reverse read is sequenced last, after the cluster has degraded.",
    "the files are named _1 (forward) and _2 (reverse) — set mate_rev <- 2.")
```

## 1.3 Expected errors — the number `maxEE` actually filters on

`filterAndTrim(maxEE = 2)` does not count bad bases. It converts each quality score
to an error probability and adds them up:

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;P(error) = 10^(−Q/10)&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;→&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;EE = Σᵢ 10^(−Qᵢ/10)

A read is discarded when its expected number of errors exceeds `maxEE`. Write that
conversion yourself:

```{webr}
# A short stretch of quality scores from a real read
Q <- c(38, 38, 37, 36, 32, 30, 28, 24, 20, 15)

# Convert Phred score -> probability that the base is wrong.
p_error <- ______             # <- blank: use Q in the formula 10^(-Q/10)

cat("Q     :", Q, "\n")
cat("P(err):", signif(p_error, 2), "\n")
cat("Expected errors in these 10 bases:", round(sum(p_error), 3), "\n\n")

cat("A Q38 base is wrong with probability", signif(10^(-38/10), 2), "\n")
cat("A Q15 base is wrong with probability", signif(10^(-15/10), 2),
    " <- one low-quality base contributes more than 100 good ones\n")

say(is.numeric(p_error) && length(p_error) == length(Q) &&
      isTRUE(all.equal(p_error, 10^(-Q/10))),
    "correct — and notice the last line: expected errors are dominated by the few worst bases, which is why trimming the tail is so effective.",
    "translate the formula directly: p_error <- 10^(-Q/10)")
```

## 1.4 Choosing the filtering parameters

Now the real decision. We ran the filter over a grid of settings on all 18 files and
recorded how many reads survive. Longer reads carry more information but accumulate
more expected errors, so retention drops.

```{webr}
r <- retention[retention$sample == "CON1", ]

# How does retention depend on where we truncate the 3' end?
tab <- r[r$trimLeft == 0 & r$maxEE == 2, c("mate", "truncLen", "pct_kept")]
print(tab[order(tab$mate, tab$truncLen), ], row.names = FALSE)

# Show the whole trade-off for the reverse reads (the harder case)
rr <- r[r$mate == 2 & r$trimLeft == 0, ]
mat <- tapply(rr$pct_kept, list(factor(rr$truncLen), factor(rr$maxEE)), max)
cat("\n% of reverse reads kept   (rows = truncLen, cols = maxEE)\n")
print(mat)

barplot(t(mat), beside = TRUE, ylim = c(0, 105),
        xlab = "truncLen (3' truncation)", ylab = "% reads kept",
        main = "CON1 reverse reads: retention vs truncation and maxEE",
        legend.text = paste("maxEE =", colnames(mat)),
        args.legend = list(x = "bottomright", bty = "n"))
```

```{webr}
# Suppose you require at least 95% of the REVERSE reads to survive with maxEE = 2.
# Read it off the table above and enter the longest truncLen that still qualifies.
my_truncLen <- ______          # <- blank

r2 <- retention[retention$sample == "CON1" & retention$mate == 2 &
                  retention$trimLeft == 0 & retention$maxEE == 2, ]
got <- r2$pct_kept[r2$truncLen == my_truncLen]
cat("truncLen =", my_truncLen, "keeps", got, "% of the reverse reads\n")

say(length(got) == 1 && got >= 95 &&
      !any(r2$pct_kept[r2$truncLen > my_truncLen] >= 95),
    paste0("right — truncating at ", my_truncLen, " keeps ", got,
           "% while preserving as much sequence as possible. Truncating further would keep more reads but throw away real sequence you paid for."),
    "look at the maxEE = 2 column: 150 keeps ~90%, 125 keeps ~94%, 100 keeps ~97%. Which is the LONGEST that reaches 95%?")
```

::: {.run-local}
**Run the filter with the parameters you just chose.** Back in RStudio on ERDA:

```r
# Build the sample names (see Session 2.1 for how this line is put together)
sample.names <- paste(sapply(strsplit(basename(fnFs), "_"), `[`, 1),
                      sapply(strsplit(basename(fnFs), "_"), `[`, 2), sep = "_")

filtFs <- file.path(path, "filtered", paste0(sample.names, "_F_filt.fastq.gz"))
filtRs <- file.path(path, "filtered", paste0(sample.names, "_R_filt.fastq.gz"))
names(filtFs) <- sample.names
names(filtRs) <- sample.names

out <- filterAndTrim(fnFs, filtFs, fnRs, filtRs,
                     trimLeft   = 10,             # drop the noisy first cycles
                     truncLen   = c(150, 125),    # forward, reverse  <- your choice
                     maxEE      = c(2, 2),
                     truncQ     = 2, minLen = 35, rm.phix = TRUE,
                     compress   = TRUE, multithread = FALSE)
out                                                # reads.in vs reads.out per sample
```

Compare the `reads.out` column with the percentages you read off the table above —
they should agree closely.
:::

# Session 2 — Read mapping and the count table {#sec-mapping}
[Wednesday 23-09]{.session-chip}

::: {.run-local}
**kallisto runs in a terminal, not in R.** Open a Terminal on ERDA. You need the
transcript FASTA and your filtered reads from Session 1.

```bash
# 1. Build the index once (takes a few minutes)
kallisto index -i C_fructicola_GSE103878.idx GSE103878_1104.transcripts.fasta

# 2. Quantify one sample (paired-end: forward file then reverse file)
mkdir -p results
kallisto quant -i C_fructicola_GSE103878.idx -o ./results/APP1 -t 2 \
    APP1_SRR6041847_F_filt.fastq.gz APP1_SRR6041847_R_filt.fastq.gz

# 3. Repeat for every sample. Each run writes results/<SAMPLE>/abundance.tsv
```

Useful terminal commands: `cd dirname` (enter a directory), `cd ..` (go up),
`ls -al` (list with detail), `mkdir xx` (create), `pwd` (where am I).

If your run does not finish, Absalon has the finished output:
`abundance_files_from_kallisto.zip`.
:::

This is what kallisto produced for the nine samples — one `abundance.tsv` each,
17,827 transcripts per file:

```{webr}
print(kal, row.names = FALSE)
cat("\nEach abundance.tsv has one row per transcript and these columns:\n")
cat("  target_id | length | eff_length | est_counts | tpm\n\n")
cat("total_est_counts differs a lot between samples (sequencing depth),\n")
cat("but total_tpm is 1e6 in every one — that is what TPM means.\n")
```

::: {.provenance}
Look at the `file_md5` column: **CON1 and CON2 have the same checksum.** The two files
in `abundance_files_from_kallisto.zip` are byte-identical — CON2 is a duplicate of
CON1. This is a real error in the course material, not a trick, and §2.3 below shows
you how to catch it. (The main count table used from Session 3 onwards is unaffected:
its CON1 and CON2 columns are genuinely different.)
:::

## 2.1 The sample-name puzzle

Before you can combine 9 output files you need 9 clean sample names. This is the
same `paste` sequence as in the 2025 exercise — work through it and see why each
attempt fails.

```{webr}
fnames <- c("APP1small_SRR6041847_1.fastq.gz", "APP2small_SRR6041848_1.fastq.gz",
            "CON1small_SRR6041844_1.fastq.gz", "CON2small_SRR6041845_1.fastq.gz")

# strsplit() cuts each name at every "_" and returns a LIST of pieces
strsplit(fnames, "_")[[1]]

# take the 1st and 2nd piece of each name
part1 <- sapply(strsplit(fnames, "_"), function(x) x[1])
part2 <- sapply(strsplit(fnames, "_"), function(x) x[2])
part1
part2

cat("\nc()      :", c(part1, part2)[1:4], "...  <- stacks them, 8 elements. No.\n")
cat("paste()  :", paste(part1, part2)[1],  "        <- joined with a SPACE. No.\n")
cat("paste0() :", paste0(part1, part2)[1], "         <- no separator at all. No.\n")
```

```{webr}
# Join the two pieces with an underscore between them.
sample.names <- paste(part1, part2, sep = ______)     # <- blank

print(sample.names)

say(is.character(sample.names) && length(sample.names) == 4 &&
      sample.names[1] == "APP1small_SRR6041847",
    'that is it — paste(..., sep = "_") gives APP1small_SRR6041847. sapply/strsplit/paste is the standard way to turn file names into sample names.',
    'paste() takes a sep argument: sep = "_"')
```

## 2.2 One abundance table

```{webr}
app1 <- read.csv("data/abundance/APP1_abundance.csv")
head(app1)

cat("\nrows in this file:", nrow(app1), "\n")
cat("est_counts = estimated reads assigned to the transcript\n")
cat("eff_length = transcript length corrected for the fragment-length distribution\n")
cat("tpm        = transcripts per million, length- AND depth-normalised\n\n")

# NOTE: to keep this page fast these files hold a 3,000-transcript subset of the
# 17,827 kallisto reported, so their TPM does NOT sum to 1e6 — only the full file does.
cat("TPM summed over this 3,000-transcript subset:", round(sum(app1$tpm)), "\n")
cat("TPM summed over the full 17,827-transcript file:",
    round(kal$total_tpm[kal$sample == "APP1"]), "  <- 1e6, as TPM must be\n")
```

## 2.3 Building the count matrix

The count table is just the `est_counts` column of every sample, glued side by side
and keyed on `target_id`.

```{webr}
samps <- c("CON1","CON2","CON3","APP1","APP2","APP3","CIH1","CIH2","CIH3")

tables <- list()
for (s in samps) {
  tables[[s]] <- read.csv(paste0("data/abundance/", s, "_abundance.csv"))
}

# Every file lists the same transcripts in the same order, so we can take the ids once
gene_ids <- tables[[1]]$target_id
all_same <- all(sapply(tables, function(x) identical(x$target_id, gene_ids)))
cat("all files in the same transcript order:", all_same, "\n")

# Pull the SAME column out of each table and bind the columns together.
count_matrix <- sapply(tables, function(x) x$______)   # <- blank

rownames(count_matrix) <- gene_ids
cat("count matrix:", nrow(count_matrix), "transcripts x", ncol(count_matrix), "samples\n\n")
print(round(head(count_matrix, 4)))

say(is.matrix(count_matrix) && ncol(count_matrix) == 9 &&
      isTRUE(all.equal(unname(count_matrix[, "APP1"]), tables[["APP1"]]$est_counts)),
    "correct — est_counts is the column DESeq2 needs. Building the matrix is just 'take the same column from every file'.",
    "DESeq2 wants raw counts, not TPM. Which column is that? x$est_counts")
```

## 2.4 Check the matrix before you trust it

Never hand a count matrix to DESeq2 without looking at it. The cheapest check is
whether any two columns are identical — biological replicates never are.

```{webr}
# Correlate every sample against every other on the log scale
cm <- cor(log2(count_matrix + 1))
round(cm, 3)

# Flag any pair of columns that is EXACTLY identical
dup <- which(duplicated(t(count_matrix)))
if (length(dup) > 0) {
  for (j in dup) {
    same <- which(apply(count_matrix, 2, function(cc) identical(cc, count_matrix[, j])))
    cat("\n⚠  identical columns:", paste(colnames(count_matrix)[same], collapse = " == "), "\n")
  }
} else cat("\nno duplicated columns\n")
```

`CON1` and `CON2` come out identical, with a correlation of exactly 1. Two biological
replicates cannot be identical to the last decimal, so this is a file-handling
mistake, not biology — the same file was copied twice when the archive was made. Had
you run DESeq2 on this matrix it would have reported an impossibly small within-group
variance for CON and inflated your significance. **This is why you look first.**

## 2.5 Why DESeq2 wants counts, not TPM

```{webr}
tpm_matrix <- sapply(tables, function(x) x$tpm)
rownames(tpm_matrix) <- gene_ids

cat("Column sums of est_counts — sequencing depth differs a lot between samples:\n")
print(round(colSums(count_matrix)))
cat("\nOver the FULL transcriptome, TPM is normalised to 1e6 in every sample:\n")
print(setNames(round(kal$total_tpm), kal$sample))
```

TPM has already had library size divided out, so every sample sums to the same total.
That is convenient for eyeballing expression, but it destroys the information DESeq2
needs: **how many reads** a measurement is based on. A gene at 50 TPM in a 40-million
read sample is far more reliable than the same 50 TPM in a 2-million read sample, and
only the raw counts still know the difference. That is why the next session starts
from `est_counts`.

# Session 3 — Differential expression {#sec-de}
[Monday 28-09]{.session-chip}

From here on we use the **full** count matrix — all 12 samples including the infected
leaf (IL), all 17,827 genes, mapped with Bowtie2 and counted with HTSeq as described
in Liang et al. 2018.

```{webr}
dim(CNT)
CNT[1:4, 1:6]
data.frame(sample = samples, condition = condition)
```

## 3.1 Library size

```{webr}
depth <- colSums(CNT)

barplot(depth / 1e6, col = cond_col[condition], las = 2,
        ylab = "Million mapped reads", main = "Library size per sample")
legend("topright", names(cond_col), fill = cond_col, bty = "n")

print(data.frame(sample = samples, condition = condition,
                 million_reads = round(depth / 1e6, 2)), row.names = FALSE)
```

The three IL samples are dramatically smaller. Hold that thought — §3.3 explains it.

## 3.2 Estimate the size factors yourself

This is the single most useful thing to understand about DESeq2, and it is five lines
of base R. DESeq2 does **not** normalise by total reads (one runaway gene would drag
every other gene down). It uses the **median-of-ratios**:

1. for each gene, compute its geometric mean across all samples — a synthetic
   "reference sample";
2. for each sample, divide every gene by that reference;
3. the sample's size factor is the **median** of those ratios.

Because it is a median, a handful of extreme genes cannot move it.

```{webr}
log_cnt <- log(CNT)                     # log of every count; zeros become -Inf
ref     <- rowMeans(log_cnt)            # log geometric mean per gene
keep    <- is.finite(ref)               # drop genes with a zero in ANY sample
cat("genes usable as reference:", sum(keep), "of", nrow(CNT), "\n")

ratios <- log_cnt[keep, ] - ref[keep]   # log ratio of each sample to the reference

# Take the summary statistic that makes this robust to outliers.
my_sf <- exp(apply(ratios, 2, ______))  # <- blank

comparison <- data.frame(sample = samples,
                         mine   = round(my_sf, 4),
                         deseq2 = sf_deseq$size_factor[match(samples, sf_deseq$sample)])
print(comparison, row.names = FALSE)

say(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(round(my_sf, 3)),
                     unname(round(sf_deseq$size_factor[match(samples, sf_deseq$sample)], 3)))),
    "your size factors match DESeq2's to three decimals. You have just reimplemented estimateSizeFactors() in five lines of base R.",
    "the whole point is robustness to outliers - use median, not mean.")
```

```{webr}
# Normalise and see what changed
NORM <- sweep(CNT, 2, my_sf, "/")

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
boxplot(log2(CNT + 1), col = cond_col[condition], las = 2, outline = FALSE,
        main = "Raw counts", ylab = "log2(count + 1)")
boxplot(log2(NORM + 1), col = cond_col[condition], las = 2, outline = FALSE,
        main = "Size-factor normalised", ylab = "log2(normalised + 1)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## 3.3 Why are the IL samples so different?

```{webr}
print(data.frame(sample = samples, condition = condition,
                 million_reads = round(depth / 1e6, 2),
                 size_factor   = round(my_sf, 3)), row.names = FALSE)

cat("\nmean size factor by condition:\n")
print(round(tapply(my_sf, condition, mean), 3))
```

The IL size factors are roughly **0.10–0.27** against ~2.5 for APP: an order of
magnitude. The reason is biological, not technical. IL is RNA extracted from an
*infected apple leaf*, so most of the RNA in the tube is **apple**, not fungus. Only
a small fraction of the reads map to the *C. fructicola* transcriptome, so the fungal
library is effectively tiny. This is exactly what size factors are for — but it also
means IL carries much less statistical power, and comparisons involving it should be
read with that in mind.

## 3.4 Variance stabilisation

Raw RNAseq counts are heteroscedastic: highly expressed genes vary more in absolute
terms, so a plain log transform leaves low-count genes looking noisiest. `vst()`
corrects this. Compare the mean–SD relationship before and after.

```{webr}
sub  <- CNT[rowSums(CNT) >= 10, ]         # the genes DESeq2 kept
lsub <- log2(sub + 1)

m_log <- rowMeans(lsub);      s_log <- apply(lsub, 1, sd)
m_vst <- rowMeans(VST);       s_vst <- apply(VST,  1, sd)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(m_log, s_log, pch = 20, cex = 0.3, col = adjustcolor("grey30", 0.25),
     xlab = "mean log2(count + 1)", ylab = "standard deviation",
     main = "log2(count + 1)", ylim = c(0, 4))
lines(lowess(m_log, s_log), col = "red", lwd = 2.5)
plot(m_vst, s_vst, pch = 20, cex = 0.3, col = adjustcolor("grey30", 0.25),
     xlab = "mean VST value", ylab = "standard deviation",
     main = "vst()", ylim = c(0, 4))
lines(lowess(m_vst, s_vst), col = "red", lwd = 2.5)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

A perfect transformation gives a **flat** red line — SD independent of mean. The VST
panel is much flatter, which is why PCA and clustering are run on VST values and never
on raw counts.

## 3.5 Principal component analysis

```{webr}
# prcomp expects SAMPLES in rows, so transpose. Use the most variable genes.
v   <- apply(VST, 1, var)
top <- names(sort(v, decreasing = TRUE))[1:500]

# Which matrix should PCA use — the raw counts or the variance-stabilised values?
pca <- prcomp(t(______[top, ]), scale. = FALSE)     # <- blank

pct <- round(100 * pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2), 1)

plot(pca$x[, 1], pca$x[, 2], pch = 19, cex = 2.4, col = cond_col[condition],
     xlab = paste0("PC1 (", pct[1], "%)"), ylab = paste0("PC2 (", pct[2], "%)"),
     main = "PCA of the 500 most variable genes")
text(pca$x[, 1], pca$x[, 2], samples, pos = 3, cex = 0.75)
abline(h = 0, v = 0, lty = 3, col = "grey60")

cat("Variance explained by each PC (%):", pct[1:6], "\n")
cat("PC1 + PC2 =", pct[1] + pct[2], "% — the rest is spread over PC3..PC11\n")

say(exists("pca") && isTRUE(all.equal(unname(pca$sdev[1]),
      unname(prcomp(t(VST[top, ]), scale. = FALSE)$sdev[1]))),
    "correct — PCA on VST values. Replicates group together and the four growth forms separate, which is what you want to see before trusting any differential expression result.",
    "PCA must run on variance-stabilised data, not raw counts: use VST.")
```

The percentages do not add to 100 because there are 11 more components; PC1 and PC2
are simply the two directions capturing the most variance.

## 3.6 Sample-to-sample distances

```{webr}
d   <- dist(t(VST[top, ]))          # Euclidean distance between samples
dm  <- as.matrix(d)
ord <- hclust(d)$order

image(1:12, 1:12, dm[ord, ord], axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
      col = hcl.colors(32, "Blues", rev = TRUE),
      main = "Euclidean distance between samples (VST)")
axis(1, 1:12, samples[ord], las = 2, cex.axis = 0.75)
axis(2, 1:12, samples[ord], las = 2, cex.axis = 0.75)

plot(hclust(d), labels = samples, main = "Sample clustering", xlab = "", sub = "")
```

::: {.run-local}
**The DESeq2 workflow itself.** Everything above prepared you to read its output;
this is how you produce it. Files from Absalon: `C_fructicola_counts.zip`
(`GSE103878_1104.genes.count.txt` and `GSE103878_1104_genes_annot.tab`).

```r
library(DESeq2)

countdata <- read.delim("GSE103878_1104.genes.count.txt", row.names = 1)
coldata   <- data.frame(
  row.names = colnames(countdata),
  condition = factor(sub("[0-9]+$", "", colnames(countdata)))
)

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = countdata,
                              colData   = coldata,
                              design    = ~ condition)

dds <- dds[rowSums(counts(dds)) >= 10, ]      # the prefilter from §3.4
dds <- DESeq(dds)                             # size factors + dispersions + Wald test

sizeFactors(dds)                              # compare with your §3.2 values
vsd <- vst(dds, blind = FALSE)                # the VST matrix used above
plotPCA(vsd, intgroup = "condition")
plotDispEsts(dds)

res <- results(dds, contrast = c("condition", "APP", "CON"), alpha = 0.05)
summary(res)
plotMA(res)

# annotate and export
annot <- read.delim("GSE103878_1104_genes_annot.tab")
out   <- merge(as.data.frame(res), annot, by.x = "row.names", by.y = "ID", all.x = TRUE)
head(out[order(out$padj), ], 10)
```

The `res` object this produces is the table loaded as `de` in the cells below — so
your local run and this page should agree.
:::

## 3.7 Reading the results table

```{webr}
str(de)
head(de[order(de$padj), c("gene", "baseMean", "log2FoldChange", "padj", "annotation")], 8)

cat("\ngenes tested :", nrow(de), "\n")
cat("padj < 0.05  :", sum(de$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
cat("  up in APP  :", sum(de$padj < 0.05 & de$log2FoldChange > 0, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
cat("  down in APP:", sum(de$padj < 0.05 & de$log2FoldChange < 0, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
cat("NA padj      :", sum(is.na(de$padj)), " (filtered out by independent filtering)\n")
```

## 3.8 MA plot and volcano plot

```{webr}
sig <- !is.na(de$padj) & de$padj < 0.05

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
# MA: mean expression vs fold change
plot(de$baseMean, de$log2FoldChange, log = "x", pch = 20, cex = 0.35,
     col = ifelse(sig, adjustcolor("#C44E52", 0.55), adjustcolor("grey40", 0.35)),
     xlab = "mean of normalised counts", ylab = "log2 fold change (APP / CON)",
     main = "MA plot", ylim = c(-12, 12))
abline(h = 0, col = "blue", lwd = 1.5)

# Volcano: fold change vs significance
plot(de$log2FoldChange, -log10(de$pvalue), pch = 20, cex = 0.35,
     col = ifelse(sig, adjustcolor("#C44E52", 0.55), adjustcolor("grey40", 0.35)),
     xlab = "log2 fold change (APP / CON)", ylab = "-log10(p-value)",
     main = "Volcano plot", xlim = c(-12, 12))
abline(v = c(-1, 1), lty = 2, col = "grey40")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Low-expression genes fan out on the left of the MA plot: with few reads the fold
change is poorly determined, which is exactly why the `rowSums >= 10` prefilter and
DESeq2's independent filtering exist.

```{webr}
# The 10 most strongly up-regulated genes in appressoria, with their function
up <- de[sig & de$log2FoldChange > 0, ]
up <- up[order(-up$log2FoldChange), ]
print(head(up[, c("gene", "log2FoldChange", "padj", "annotation")], 10), row.names = FALSE)
```

Most of the extreme fold changes belong to hypothetical proteins — normal for a fungal
genome, and a reminder that a big log2FC is not the same as an interpretable result.

## 3.9 Comparing two contrasts

`de_cih` holds the same analysis for **CIH vs CON**. Comparing two contrasts separates
genes specific to appressoria from the general infection programme.

```{webr}
m <- merge(de[,     c("gene", "log2FoldChange", "padj")],
           de_cih[, c("gene", "log2FoldChange", "padj")],
           by = "gene", suffixes = c("_APP", "_CIH"))
m <- m[!is.na(m$padj_APP) & !is.na(m$padj_CIH), ]

plot(m$log2FoldChange_APP, m$log2FoldChange_CIH, pch = 20, cex = 0.3,
     col = adjustcolor("grey30", 0.3),
     xlab = "log2FC  APP vs CON", ylab = "log2FC  CIH vs CON",
     main = "Appressoria and infectious hyphae share much of their response")
abline(0, 1, col = "blue", lty = 2); abline(h = 0, v = 0, col = "grey60", lty = 3)

cat("correlation of the two contrasts:",
    round(cor(m$log2FoldChange_APP, m$log2FoldChange_CIH), 3), "\n\n")

app_only <- m$gene[m$padj_APP < 0.05 & m$log2FoldChange_APP >  2 &
                   (m$padj_CIH >= 0.05 | abs(m$log2FoldChange_CIH) < 1)]
cat("up in APP but NOT in CIH:", length(app_only), "genes\n")
print(head(data.frame(gene = app_only, annotation = ann[app_only]), 6), row.names = FALSE)
```

## 3.10 Multiple testing

14,099 tests at p < 0.05 would give ~700 false positives by chance alone. That is
what the adjusted p-value fixes.

```{webr}
p <- de$pvalue[!is.na(de$pvalue)]

bonf <- p.adjust(p, method = "bonferroni")
# Benjamini-Hochberg controls the false discovery rate. Enter its method name:
bh   <- p.adjust(p, method = ______)          # <- blank

cat("raw p < 0.05          :", sum(p    < 0.05), "\n")
cat("Bonferroni-adjusted   :", sum(bonf < 0.05), "\n")
cat("BH-adjusted (FDR)     :", sum(bh   < 0.05), "\n\n")
cat("expected false positives among the raw hits:", round(0.05 * length(p)), "\n")

say(isTRUE(all.equal(bh, p.adjust(p, method = "BH"))),
    'correct. Bonferroni controls the probability of even ONE false positive and is very conservative; BH controls the FRACTION of false positives among the genes you call significant (the FDR) — the right trade-off when you are screening thousands of genes. padj in a DESeq2 table is BH.',
    'the method string is "BH" (or equivalently "fdr").')
```

---

# Session 4 — Enrichment and clustering {#sec-enrich}
[Wednesday 30-09]{.session-chip}

You now have thousands of significant genes, which is not an answer to a biological
question. Enrichment analysis turns that list into statements about **function**.

Everything in this session runs here — Fisher's exact test, the hypergeometric
distribution, `hclust` and `kmeans` are all base R.

## 4.1 Defining the gene list

Enrichment starts with a decision most papers gloss over: what counts as
"differentially expressed"?

```{webr}
universe <- de$gene[!is.na(de$padj)]              # every gene actually tested
cat("universe (tested genes):", length(universe), "\n\n")

for (lfc in c(0, 1, 2, 3)) {
  n <- sum(de$padj < 0.05 & abs(de$log2FoldChange) > lfc, na.rm = TRUE)
  cat(sprintf("padj < 0.05 and |log2FC| > %d : %5d genes\n", lfc, n))
}

# We use a strict list so the enrichment is specific rather than "everything".
de_genes <- de$gene[!is.na(de$padj) & de$padj < 0.05 & de$log2FoldChange > 2]
cat("\nUp in APP with log2FC > 2:", length(de_genes), "genes\n")
```

## 4.2 The gene sets

```{webr}
head(gene_sets, 3)

sizes <- table(gene_sets$term_name)
cat(length(sizes), "functional categories\n\n")
print(sort(sizes, decreasing = TRUE))
```

::: {.provenance}
These categories were built by matching keywords against the annotation text — every
gene whose description contains `cytochrome p450`, and so on. They are real
annotations grouped by a simple rule, **not** curated GO or PFAM terms, so treat the
biology below as an exercise rather than a published result. The statistics are
identical to the real thing.
:::

## 4.3 The hypergeometric test, by hand

The lecture's question — *is the overlap larger than expected by random sampling?* —
is answered by the hypergeometric distribution. Four numbers define it:

| symbol | meaning |
|---|---|
| `k` | genes in your DE list that are in the set (the **overlap**) |
| `K` | genes in the set, in the whole universe |
| `N` | size of the universe |
| `n` | size of your DE list |

```{webr}
set_name <- "Cytochrome P450"
set_genes <- gene_sets$gene[gene_sets$term_name == set_name]

N <- length(universe)                                  # universe
n <- length(de_genes)                                  # DE list
K <- sum(set_genes %in% universe)                      # set, restricted to universe
k <- sum(de_genes %in% set_genes)                      # overlap

cat(set_name, "\n")
cat("  N (universe)     :", N, "\n")
cat("  n (DE list)      :", n, "\n")
cat("  K (in set)       :", K, "\n")
cat("  k (overlap)      :", k, "\n")
cat("  expected overlap :", round(n * K / N, 2), "\n")
cat("  fold enrichment  :", round(k / (n * K / N), 2), "\n")
# fold ~ 1 means the overlap is exactly what chance predicts — no enrichment.

# P(X >= k) — the probability of an overlap AT LEAST this large by chance.
# phyper(q, m, n, k) is P(X <= q), so we ask for the upper tail at k - 1.
p_enrich <- phyper(______, K, N - K, n, lower.tail = FALSE)   # <- blank

cat("\n  p-value          :", signif(p_enrich, 3), "\n")

say(isTRUE(all.equal(p_enrich, phyper(k - 1, K, N - K, n, lower.tail = FALSE))),
    "correct — the upper tail must start at k-1 so that the observed overlap k is itself included in 'at least k'. Using k instead is an off-by-one error that silently makes every p-value too small.",
    "you want P(X >= k). Since phyper(q, ...) with lower.tail = FALSE gives P(X > q), you must pass k - 1.")
```

```{webr}
# fisher.test on the 2x2 table gives the identical p-value
tab <- matrix(c(k,          n - k,
                K - k,      N - n - (K - k)), nrow = 2,
              dimnames = list(c("in set", "not in set"), c("in DE list", "not in DE list")))
print(tab)

cat("\nphyper      :", signif(phyper(k - 1, K, N - K, n, lower.tail = FALSE), 4), "\n")
cat("fisher.test :", signif(fisher.test(tab, alternative = "greater")$p.value, 4), "\n")
```

Fisher's exact test and the hypergeometric upper tail are the same calculation — that
is the point the lecture makes when it says Fisher's test "is based on a theoretical
null-hypothesis distribution (hypergeometric)".

## 4.4 Does your code actually work? Use a positive control

Cytochrome P450 came out at fold ≈ 1 — no enrichment at all. Before concluding
anything biological you must rule out the other explanation: **that your code is
wrong.** The way to do that is a positive control — a gene list you *know* is
enriched, built on purpose.

```{webr}
set.seed(1)
p450 <- intersect(gene_sets$gene[gene_sets$term_name == "Cytochrome P450"], universe)

# A fake "DE list": 60 real P450 genes + 240 genes drawn at random.
fake_list <- c(sample(p450, 60),
               sample(setdiff(universe, p450), 240))

nf <- length(fake_list)
Kf <- length(p450)
kf <- sum(fake_list %in% p450)

cat("planted 60 P450 genes into a list of", nf, "\n")
cat("  expected overlap by chance :", round(nf * Kf / N, 2), "\n")
cat("  observed overlap           :", kf, "\n")
cat("  fold enrichment            :", round(kf / (nf * Kf / N), 1), "\n")
cat("  p-value                    :",
    signif(phyper(kf - 1, Kf, N - Kf, nf, lower.tail = FALSE), 3), "\n")
```

The test finds it with an astronomically small p-value. **The machinery works.** So
when the real data gives nothing, that is a statement about the data, not a bug.

## 4.5 Testing every category

```{webr}
terms  <- unique(gene_sets$term_name)
N_univ <- length(universe)     # recomputed here so this cell stands on its own
n_de   <- length(de_genes)

res <- data.frame()
for (tm in terms) {
  sg <- gene_sets$gene[gene_sets$term_name == tm]
  K  <- sum(sg %in% universe)
  k  <- sum(de_genes %in% sg)
  if (K < 5) next
  res <- rbind(res, data.frame(
    term      = tm,
    set_size  = K,
    overlap   = k,
    expected  = round(n_de * K / N_univ, 2),
    fold      = round(k / (n_de * K / N_univ), 2),
    pvalue    = phyper(k - 1, K, N_univ - K, n_de, lower.tail = FALSE)
  ))
}

# Same multiple-testing problem as in §3.9 — one test per category.
res$padj <- p.adjust(res$pvalue, method = "BH")
res <- res[order(res$pvalue), ]

print(head(res, 12), row.names = FALSE)
cat("\ncategories with raw p < 0.05 :", sum(res$pvalue < 0.05), "of", nrow(res), "\n")
cat("categories with padj < 0.05  :", sum(res$padj  < 0.05), "of", nrow(res), "\n")
```

```{webr}
# Fold enrichment for every category, ranked. Nothing is far from 1.
o <- order(res$fold)
par(mar = c(5, 18, 4, 2))
barplot(res$fold[o], horiz = TRUE, names.arg = res$term[o], las = 1, cex.names = 0.7,
        col = ifelse(res$padj[o] < 0.05, "#C44E52", "#9aa7b4"),
        xlab = "Fold enrichment (1 = exactly what chance predicts)",
        xlim = c(0, 2), main = "Up in appressoria: all 29 categories")
abline(v = 1, lty = 2, lwd = 2)
par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2))
```

## 4.6 Nothing is significant. Why?

This is the most common outcome of a first real enrichment analysis, and being able
to diagnose it is worth more than a lucky hit. Four things are working against us
here, and you can check each one:

```{webr}
cat("1. The gene list is enormous.\n")
cat("   ", n, "of", N, "tested genes =", round(100 * n / N, 1),
    "% of the genome is on the list.\n")
cat("    A list that big overlaps every category at roughly the background rate,\n")
cat("    so no category can stand out. Enrichment needs a SELECTIVE list.\n\n")

cat("2. The categories are protein families, not biological processes.\n")
cat("    'Protein kinase' (", sum(gene_sets$term_name == "Protein kinase"),
    " genes) is scattered across every pathway in the cell.\n", sep = "")
cat("    Real GO terms describe processes that are switched on together;\n")
cat("    a family like 'kinase' has no reason to move as a block.\n\n")

cat("3. Only", nrow(res), "categories were tested, but BH still costs us.\n")
best <- res[which.min(res$pvalue), ]
cat("    best raw p =", signif(best$pvalue, 3), "->  padj =", signif(best$padj, 3),
    "  (", best$term, ")\n\n")

cat("4. Most of the genome has no usable annotation.\n")
cat("   ", sum(!(universe %in% gene_sets$gene)), "of", N,
    "tested genes are in no category at all\n")
cat("    (mostly 'hypothetical protein') — they can never contribute a hit.\n")
```

None of this means the appressoria have no biology. It means **this gene list against
these categories** cannot detect it. The fixes a real analysis would use are: a
selective list (top few hundred genes, or a cluster — §4.7), curated GO/PFAM
annotation instead of keyword families, and a whole-distribution method that needs no
threshold at all (§4.8).

::: {.provenance}
It would have been easy to make this page produce an impressive enrichment table by
hunting for a category and threshold that happened to pass. That is p-hacking, and it
is the single most common way enrichment analysis is abused in the literature. The
result above is what this data honestly gives.
:::

## 4.7 Clustering expression profiles

Enrichment on one gene list answers one question. Clustering first, then testing each
cluster, tells you *which programmes* the fungus runs in *which* growth form — the
analysis on the last slide of the lecture.

```{webr}
# Average the VST values within each condition -> one profile per growth form
conds <- c("CON", "APP", "CIH", "IL")
prof  <- sapply(conds, function(cd) rowMeans(VST[, condition == cd, drop = FALSE]))

# Focus on genes that actually change, and scale each gene to shape, not level
vary  <- names(sort(apply(prof, 1, var), decreasing = TRUE))[1:1500]
scaled <- t(scale(t(prof[vary, ])))

set.seed(42)
km <- kmeans(scaled, centers = 4, nstart = 25)
cat("cluster sizes:", table(km$cluster), "\n")

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (i in 1:4) {
  members <- scaled[km$cluster == i, ]
  matplot(t(members[1:min(120, nrow(members)), ]), type = "l", lty = 1,
          col = adjustcolor("grey50", 0.25), xaxt = "n",
          xlab = "", ylab = "scaled expression",
          main = paste0("Cluster ", i, "  (n = ", sum(km$cluster == i), ")"))
  lines(km$centers[i, ], col = "#C44E52", lwd = 3)
  axis(1, 1:4, conds)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

```{webr}
# Which functions are enriched in each cluster?
enrich_cluster <- function(genes_in_cluster, univ) {
  Nn <- length(univ); nn <- length(genes_in_cluster)
  out <- data.frame()
  for (tm in unique(gene_sets$term_name)) {
    sg <- gene_sets$gene[gene_sets$term_name == tm]
    K  <- sum(sg %in% univ); k <- sum(genes_in_cluster %in% sg)
    if (K < 5 || k == 0) next
    out <- rbind(out, data.frame(term = tm, overlap = k, set_size = K,
                                 fold = round(k / (nn * K / Nn), 2),
                                 pvalue = phyper(k - 1, K, Nn - K, nn, lower.tail = FALSE)))
  }
  out$padj <- p.adjust(out$pvalue, method = "BH")
  out[order(out$pvalue), ]
}

for (i in 1:4) {
  cl <- rownames(scaled)[km$cluster == i]
  e  <- enrich_cluster(cl, vary)
  peak <- conds[which.max(km$centers[i, ])]
  cat(sprintf("\n=== Cluster %d (n = %d genes, highest in %s) ===\n",
              i, length(cl), peak))
  print(head(e[, c("term", "overlap", "set_size", "fold", "pvalue", "padj")], 3),
        row.names = FALSE)
  cat("  significant after BH:", sum(e$padj < 0.05), "\n")
}
```

A cluster is a much more coherent list than "everything with padj < 0.05" — these
genes were selected *because* they share an expression profile — and the fold
enrichments do rise. Some categories reach raw p ≈ 0.015, which is suggestive: the
CON-peaking cluster leans towards cytochrome P450 and heterokaryon-incompatibility
genes. But none survives correction, so the honest way to report this is as a
hypothesis to test, never as a finding.

## 4.8 How much does the threshold matter?

The lecture's argument for whole-distribution methods like GSEA is that
threshold-based tests give different answers at different cut-offs. Test that claim.

```{webr}
Nu <- length(universe)

for (lfc in c(1, 2, 3)) {
  dg <- de$gene[!is.na(de$padj) & de$padj < 0.05 & de$log2FoldChange > lfc]
  nn <- length(dg)
  out <- data.frame()
  for (tm in unique(gene_sets$term_name)) {
    sg <- gene_sets$gene[gene_sets$term_name == tm]
    K  <- sum(sg %in% universe); k <- sum(dg %in% sg)
    if (K < 5) next
    out <- rbind(out, data.frame(term = tm,
                 p = phyper(k - 1, K, Nu - K, nn, lower.tail = FALSE)))
  }
  out$padj <- p.adjust(out$p, method = "BH")
  out <- out[order(out$p), ]
  cat(sprintf("\nlog2FC > %d  (%d genes)  -> %d significant after BH, best raw p = %.3f\n",
              lfc, nn, sum(out$padj < 0.05), min(out$p)))
  cat("   top 3 by raw p:", paste(head(out$term, 3), collapse = " | "), "\n")
}
```

The ranking reshuffles as the threshold moves — a different cut-off would have given
you a different "top hit" to write about. Nothing is wrong with any single run; the
point is that the threshold is a **choice you are making**, and it belongs in your
methods section.

This is exactly the argument the lecture makes for **whole-distribution methods**:
there is no natural value for the cut-off, different settings give different results,
and thresholding throws away the difference between a strong and a weak signal. GSEA
avoids the problem by ranking *every* gene and asking where a set's members fall in
that ranking, rather than cutting the list in two. It needs packages that webR cannot
load (`fgsea`, `clusterProfiler`), so it belongs in the local block below.

::: {.run-local}
**Real enrichment analysis, in RStudio.** With curated annotation and a proper tool:

```r
# Over-representation (what you did by hand above), with real GO terms
library(clusterProfiler)
ego <- enrichGO(gene = de_gene_ids, universe = all_gene_ids,
                OrgDb = org.Xx.eg.db, ont = "BP",
                pAdjustMethod = "BH", qvalueCutoff = 0.05)
dotplot(ego, showCategory = 20)

# GSEA — no threshold: rank every gene by the DESeq2 statistic
library(fgsea)
ranks <- setNames(res$stat, rownames(res))       # or -log10(pvalue) * sign(log2FC)
fg <- fgsea(pathways = gene_set_list, stats = ranks, minSize = 10, maxSize = 500)
head(fg[order(fg$padj), ])
plotEnrichment(gene_set_list[["GO:0006979"]], ranks)   # the running ES score
```

For a genome without an OrgDb — like *C. fructicola* — you would get GO or PFAM terms
from InterProScan or eggNOG-mapper output and pass them to `fgsea` as a named list.
:::

[Monday 05-10 · hand-in 15:00]{.session-chip}

::: {.run-local}
**The 2nd group assignment is a written report and must be done in RStudio.** It uses
a different organism — *Coccidioides posadasii*, the fungus causing Valley Fever — and
asks about the transcription factor Ryp1 and spherule formation.

Files on Absalon (Module 2 → Group Work):

::: {.filelist}
GroupAssignment2025.html &nbsp;&nbsp;— the questions<br>
CountTable_GroupExercise2025.csv &nbsp;&nbsp;— counts, 4 conditions x 2 replicates<br>
Annot_GroupExercise2025.csv &nbsp;&nbsp;— gene annotations
:::

Note both CSVs are **semicolon**-separated:

```r
counts <- read.csv2("CountTable_GroupExercise2025.csv", row.names = 1)
annot  <- read.csv2("Annot_GroupExercise2025.csv")
```

You hand in an **Rmarkdown document** with every group member's name at the top,
covering: a PCA of rlog values and a heatmap of VST sample distances; the prefilter
and DESeq2 run with dispersion plot and size factors; genes up in WT spherules vs WT
hyphae; and the expression of the virulence factor **SOWgp** across all four
conditions.
:::

Everything you need for it you have already done on this page — only the organism
changes:

| Assignment asks for | Practise it in |
|---|---|
| PCA of transformed values | [§3.5](#sec-de) |
| Heatmap of sample distances | [§3.6](#sec-de) |
| Prefilter + DESeq2 run | [§3.2](#sec-de), the local block in [§3.6](#sec-de) |
| Size factors, smallest library | [§3.2](#sec-de), [§3.3](#sec-de) |
| Genes up in one condition | [§3.7](#sec-de), [§3.8](#sec-de) |
| Expression of one named gene | below |

```{webr}
# Plot the normalised counts of a single gene across all conditions —
# the last question of the assignment, done here on the C. fructicola data.
NORM <- sweep(CNT, 2, sf_deseq$size_factor[match(samples, sf_deseq$sample)], "/")

# the most strongly up-regulated gene in appressoria
sig_de   <- de[!is.na(de$padj) & de$padj < 0.05, ]
top_gene <- sig_de$gene[which.max(sig_de$log2FoldChange)]

# +1 so that genes switched completely off in a condition still plot on a log axis
vals <- NORM[top_gene, ] + 1
stripchart(vals ~ factor(condition, levels = c("CON", "APP", "CIH", "IL")),
           vertical = TRUE, pch = 19, cex = 1.6, method = "jitter",
           col = cond_col[c("CON", "APP", "CIH", "IL")], log = "y",
           ylab = "normalised count + 1", xlab = "",
           main = paste("Gene", top_gene))
mtext(ann[[top_gene]], side = 3, line = 0.2, cex = 0.85)

cat("gene              :", top_gene, "\n")
cat("annotation        :", ann[[top_gene]], "\n")
cat("log2FC APP vs CON :", round(sig_de$log2FoldChange[sig_de$gene == top_gene], 2), "\n")
cat("normalised counts :\n")
print(round(NORM[top_gene, ], 1))
```
